content.text:
The Keeper's Last Light

For forty-one years, Elias Moreau climbed the one hundred and twelve iron steps of Gull Point Lighthouse every evening at dusk. He wound the clockwork, trimmed the wick, and watched the great lens begin to turn. Ships passed by in the night, and not one of them ever knew his name.

When the Coast Guard announced the light would be automated, Elias said little. He simply kept climbing.

On his final night, a fog rolled in thick as wool. The foghorn moaned, but Elias knew it could not reach the rocks that waited below the cliffs. He lit the lamp one last time and sat on the cold iron floor beside the lens, listening to the sea.

Near midnight, he heard a faint sound: the rhythmic splash of oars. A small fishing boat, its engine dead, drifted toward the rocks. A young man stood in the bow, waving a lantern that flickered weakly against the gray.

Elias stood, his knees aching, and turned the lens by hand, sweeping its beam across the water again and again. The fisherman steered toward the glow, guided past the teeth of the reef and into the calm harbor beyond.

At dawn, the fog lifted. The young man came up the steps with a loaf of bread and a thermos of coffee. "You saved us," he said.

Elias smiled and looked out at the sea. "No," he said. "The light did. I just kept it company."

Her mother had taught her to hunt by listening, to read the tracks of mice and rabbits like words on a page. But the snow had hidden everything. There were no tracks left to read, only smooth white drifts that swallowed the old trails.

The Fox Who Tried to Count Snow

The first snow came early to the Hollow Pine, and Ember, a red fox with one torn ear and a grudge against the weather, poked her nose out of her den and recoiled. The world had been erased. Everything was white, including the parts that should not be white, like the stump she had been napping on.

Her mother had taught her to hunt by listening, to read tracks like a newspaper. But the snow had buried every track in the forest, and Ember had no idea how to read a newspaper that had been replaced by a blank sheet of paper.

"Fine," she said to nobody. "I'll count instead."

She counted the hops from the oak to the stream: forty-one, though one of them was a face-plant. She counted the chickadees at the farmhouse feeder: seven, plus one loud jay who arrived late, ate everything, and called her a "fancy rat" on his way out. She counted the number of times she had slipped on ice that morning: eleven. She was not proud of that number.

On the ninth night, the moon hung round and bright over the frozen field. Ember crouched at the edge of the wood, tail wrapped around her paws, and waited for the farmer's dog to finish its nightly barking routine. It barked at the mailbox. It barked at the moon. It once barked at its own reflection in the water trough for a full twenty minutes.

Then, silence.

Ember took a breath and launched herself across the snowy field in a graceful arc of pure determination. She landed directly in a drift, disappeared completely, and burst back out like a cork from a bottle, covered in snow from ear to tail.

Somewhere in the distance, the jay laughed.

Ember shook herself off, sneezed twice, and trotted toward the henhouse with her head held high. Her plan had gone terribly, but she had one important thing to show for it. She had counted the snow, and it had counted her right back.
